blocks.text: OS-level isolation long predates Docker: chroot restricted a process's filesystem view, FreeBSD Jails and Solaris Zones added isolated users, processes and networking, all sharing one kernel.

rows: Not a security boundary; root can escape; processes, network and users shared

blocks.text: $ sudo chroot /srv/rootfs /bin/sh     # new filesystem root, same everything else

items: Isolation can live in the kernel without a hypervisor.
A container is "an OS image + isolated processes on a shared kernel".
The shared kernel is always the weak point for security.

blocks.text: chroot is not a sandbox: a root process can break out, and it doesn't isolate PIDs, networks or users. Container runtimes use pivot_root plus namespaces instead.

Q: "Did Docker invent containers?" A: "No. OS-level isolation existed in chroot, FreeBSD Jails, Solaris Zones, OpenVZ and LXC. Docker's contribution was the developer workflow: images, layers, the Dockerfile, registries and a simple CLI that made those kernel features usable and portable."

items: chroot = filesystem view only, not security.
Jails and Zones were real OS-level containers.
All share one kernel; that's the trade-off.
